questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: What is the quantum number n of a particle of mass m confined to a one-dimensional box of length L when its energy is 2h^2/mL^2?
questions.solution: E_n = n^2h^2/(8mL^2). Equating gives n^2/8 = 2, so n^2 = 16 and n = 4.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A particle of mass m is confined in a one-dimensional infinite potential well of width L. What happens to the energy levels if the width of the well is doubled?
options: The energy levels decrease by a factor of 4.
The energy levels increase by a factor of 4.
The energy levels decrease by a factor of 2.
questions.solution: E_n = n^2h^2/(8mL^2), so E ∝ 1/L^2. Doubling L divides every level by 4.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A particle is confined in a one-dimensional infinite potential well of width L. If the width of the well is doubled while the quantum number remains unchanged, its energy becomes
questions.solution: E_n ∝ 1/L^2. Doubling L multiplies the energy by (1/2)^2 = 0.25.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: What is the minimum uncertainty in the velocity of an electron if the uncertainty in its position is 50 pm?

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: An electron and a proton are accelerated through the same potential. The ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths λe/λp is
questions.solution: Both acquire the same kinetic energy qV. Since λ = h/sqrt(2mE), λ ∝ 1/sqrt(m). Hence λe/λp = sqrt(mp/me).

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Which of the following is not acceptable as a physical wave function?
options: A single-valued, finite and continuous function that is square-integrable
A continuous function whose first derivative is finite everywhere
A function that diverges at x = 0 and is discontinuous there
A complex-valued function that is normalizable
questions.solution: A physically acceptable wave function must be finite, single-valued, continuous and normalizable. A function that diverges and is discontinuous at x = 0 cannot be normalized and is therefore not acceptable.
questions.note: The original options were images; the choices here restate the criteria tested, with the answer taken from the official key.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: The principal significance of the Davisson-Germer experiment is that it provided direct experimental evidence for
questions.solution: The experiment diffracted electrons from a nickel crystal and matched the measured wavelengths with the de Broglie relation, confirming the wave nature of matter.

images.alt: Davisson-Germer apparatus and the measured diffraction polar plot.
images.caption: Davisson-Germer apparatus and the measured diffraction polar plot.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: For a one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator, the ratio of the energy of the third excited state to that of the first excited state is
questions.solution: E_v = (v + 1/2)ħω. Third excited state (v = 3): 7/2 ħω. First excited state (v = 1): 3/2 ħω. Ratio = 7/3.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: An electron is confined in an infinite potential well of width 0.2 nm. Find the speed of the electron in the n = 1 state.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A quantum simple harmonic oscillator consists of an electron bound by a restoring force proportional to its displacement, with force constant k = 8.99 N/m. What is the longest wavelength of light that can excite the oscillator?
questions.solution: The longest wavelength corresponds to the smallest energy gap, ΔE = ħω with ω = sqrt(k/m). ω = sqrt(8.99/9.11×10^-31) = 3.14×10^15 rad/s, so ΔE = 1.055×10^-34 × 3.14×10^15 = 3.31×10^-19 J. Then λ = hc/ΔE = (6.626×10^-34 × 3×10^8)/3.31×10^-19 ≈ 6.0×10^-7 m = 600 nm.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: (a) What are the mathematical features of a wave function? (b) Write the mathematical expression that ensures the total probability of finding the particle in all space is 1.
questions.solution: (a) ψ may be real or complex; it must be finite, single-valued and continuous everywhere; its first spatial derivative must be finite and continuous; and it must be square-integrable (normalizable). (b) Normalization condition: ∫ over all space |ψ(x)|^2 dx = 1.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A wave function is given by ψ(x) = A for 0 ≤ x ≤ L and zero elsewhere. Find the normalization constant A.
questions.solution: Normalization requires ∫0^L |A|^2 dx = 1, so |A|^2 L = 1 and A = 1/sqrt(L) (taking A real and positive).

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A 0.50 kg baseball is confined between two rigid walls of a stadium that can be modelled as a box of length 100 m. Calculate the minimum speed of the baseball.
questions.solution: E1 = h^2/(8mL^2) = (6.626×10^-34)^2/(8 × 0.5 × 100^2) = 1.10×10^-71 J. Then v = sqrt(2E1/m) = sqrt(2 × 1.10×10^-71/0.5) ≈ 6.6×10^-36 m/s. The result is immeasurably small, showing why quantum effects are invisible for macroscopic objects.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: The probability of finding a certain quantum particle on the x-axis between x = 4 nm and x = 7 nm is 48%. The particle's wave function ψ(x) is constant over this range. What numerical value can be attributed to ψ(x), in units of nm^-1/2?
questions.solution: P = |ψ|^2 Δx, so |ψ|^2 × 3 nm = 0.48. Hence |ψ|^2 = 0.16 nm^-1 and ψ = 0.4 nm^-1/2 (up to an arbitrary phase).

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.topic: Particle in a box - energy levels
questions.question: An electron is confined between two impenetrable walls that are 0.20 nm apart. Determine the energy levels for the states n = 1 and n = 2.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Obtain an expression for the change in barrier width required to double the tunnelling probability, assuming all other parameters remain the same. Hint: T = exp(-2CL). Express the final result in terms of C.
questions.solution: Let T1 = e^(-2CL1). For double the probability, T2 = 2T1 = e^(-2CL2). Taking logarithms: -2CL2 = ln 2 - 2CL1, so L2 - L1 = -ln 2/(2C). The barrier must be reduced by ΔL = ln2/(2C) ≈ 0.347/C to double the tunnelling probability.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Using the expression for a wave packet corresponding to a free particle, arrive at the free-particle Schrodinger equation.
questions.solution: Superpose plane waves ψ(x,t) = ∫ A(k) e^{i(kx-ωt)} dk. For a free particle E = p^2/2m with p = ħk and E = ħω, so ω = ħk^2/2m. Differentiating with respect to x gives ∂ψ/∂x = ∫ ikA e^{i(kx-ωt)}dk and ∂²ψ/∂x² = -∫ k²A e^{i(kx-ωt)}dk; differentiating with respect to t gives ∂ψ/∂t = -i∫ ωA e^{i(kx-ωt)}dk. Using ħω = ħ²k²/2m, iħ ∂ψ/∂t = -(ħ²/2m) ∂²ψ/∂x², which is the free-particle Schrodinger equation.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: How did the Davisson-Germer experiment validate the de Broglie hypothesis? Explain.
questions.solution: Electrons accelerated through a known potential were scattered from a nickel crystal and showed a pronounced diffraction maximum at a particular angle. Bragg's law gave the wavelength responsible for the diffraction, and it agreed with λ = h/sqrt(2meV) from de Broglie. This agreement established the wave nature of electrons and confirmed wave-particle duality.

images.alt: Davisson-Germer apparatus and the measured diffraction polar plot.
images.caption: Davisson-Germer apparatus and the measured diffraction polar plot.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Show that the wave function of a particle trapped in a finite potential well decays exponentially with distance outside the well.
questions.solution: Outside the well, U = U0 > E. The time-independent Schrodinger equation becomes d²ψ/dx² = (2m(U0 - E)/ħ²)ψ = α²ψ with α = sqrt(2m(U0 - E))/ħ. The solutions are ψ = A e^{αx} + B e^{-αx}. In the left region B = 0 to keep ψ finite as x → -∞, and in the right region A = 0 as x → +∞. Hence ψ ∝ e^{-α|x|}, an exponential decay into the classically forbidden region.

images.alt: Finite potential well of height U and width L, with a bound state at energy E.
images.caption: Finite potential well of height U and width L, with a bound state at energy E.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A metal surface is illuminated with monochromatic light of wavelength λ, causing the emission of photoelectrons. The stopping potential required to halt the most energetic photoelectrons is V1. If the wavelength of the incident light is halved, which statement is correct regarding the new stopping potential V2?
questions.solution: eV = hc/λ - φ. At λ/2: eV2 = 2hc/λ - φ = 2(hc/λ - φ) + φ = 2eV1 + φ. Therefore V2 = 2V1 + φ/e > 2V1.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: (a) Sketch a schematic graph of photoelectric current versus applied voltage for the photoelectric effect. Explain the significance of the point where the graph intersects the x-axis. (b) Sketch a schematic graph of the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons versus the frequency of incident light. Explain the significance of the slope and y-intercept of the graph.
questions.solution: (a) The current rises with positive voltage and saturates; for negative voltage it falls to zero at -Vs. The x-intercept (-Vs) is the stopping potential, the minimum retarding potential that stops even the most energetic photoelectrons. It is independent of light intensity. (b) Kmax versus frequency is a straight line. The slope equals Planck's constant h; the y-intercept equals -φ, where φ is the work function, so no emission occurs below the threshold frequency f0 = φ/h.

images.alt: Photoelectric current versus applied voltage at two intensities.
images.caption: Photoelectric current versus applied voltage at two intensities.

images.alt: Maximum photoelectron kinetic energy versus frequency for three metals.
images.caption: Maximum photoelectron kinetic energy versus frequency for three metals.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: When a photosensitive metal is illuminated by light of a certain wavelength, the stopping potential required to stop the ejected photoelectrons is 1.1 V. If the incident wavelength is half the threshold wavelength of the metal, find (a) the threshold frequency, (b) the work function of the metal and (c) the maximum velocity of the ejected electrons.
questions.solution: With λ = λ0/2, f = 2f0. Einstein's equation gives eV = h(2f0) - hf0 = hf0, so f0 = eV/h = (1.6×10^-19 × 1.1)/(6.626×10^-34) = 2.66×10^14 Hz. Work function φ = hf0 = 1.76×10^-19 J = 1.1 eV. Maximum speed v = sqrt(2eV/m) = sqrt(2 × 1.6×10^-19 × 1.1 / 9.11×10^-31) ≈ 6.2×10^5 m/s.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 430 nm and intensity 5 mW/m² falls on a metal surface of area 2 cm². The stopping potential for the most energetic photoelectrons is 0.80 V. Estimate the work function of the metal. If 20% of the incident photons eject electrons (quantum efficiency), estimate the photocurrent.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: State and compare four predictions of classical wave theory for the photoelectric effect with the corresponding experimental observations.
questions.solution: 1. Classical: emission should occur at any frequency if intensity is large enough. Observed: no emission below a threshold frequency, however intense the light. 2. Classical: maximum kinetic energy should increase with intensity. Observed: Kmax is independent of intensity. 3. Classical: there should be a measurable time lag before emission. Observed: emission is practically instantaneous. 4. Classical: Kmax should not depend on frequency. Observed: Kmax increases linearly with frequency, Kmax = hf - φ.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: The radius of the Sun is 6.96 × 10^8 m and its total power output is 3.85 × 10^26 W. Assuming the Sun's surface emits as a black body, calculate its surface temperature.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A radiometer measures thermal radiation from an object at 1278 K. It is set to detect peak emission and records radiation in a wavelength interval of 12.6 nm. What is the radiation intensity within this range?
questions.solution: Wien's law gives the peak wavelength: λm = b/T = 2.898×10^-3/1278 = 2.268×10^-6 m. Using Planck's spectral exitance Mλ = (2πhc²/λ^5)/(e^{hc/λkT} - 1): hc/λkT = 4.97, so the denominator is 143.5. Mλ ≈ 4.39×10^10 W/m³. The intensity in Δλ = 12.6 nm = 1.26×10^-8 m is Mλ Δλ ≈ 5.5×10^2 W/m².
questions.note: Assumes the radiometer measures spectral exitance per unit area; the accepted key awards full marks for using Planck's law with the peak wavelength.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: What is the ultraviolet catastrophe? Explain with the help of the necessary equation and a diagram.
questions.solution: The Rayleigh-Jeans law, I(λ,T)dλ = (2πckBT/λ^4)dλ, agrees with experiment only at long wavelengths. It predicts that the emitted intensity rises without limit as λ → 0, so the total radiated energy would be infinite. This divergence at short wavelengths is the ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck resolved it by assuming quantized oscillators, which gives the Planck distribution that falls to zero at short wavelengths.

images.alt: Rayleigh-Jeans law compared with the experimental blackbody spectrum.
images.caption: Rayleigh-Jeans law compared with the experimental blackbody spectrum.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A blackbody is heated from 300 K to 600 K. How will its total emitted power and peak wavelength change? Explain with the help of the necessary equations.
questions.solution: By Stefan-Boltzmann, P = σAT^4, so doubling T multiplies the power by 2^4 = 16. By Wien's law, λmT = constant, so doubling T halves the peak wavelength (λm becomes 1/2 of its original value).

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: What is the maximum change in the wavelength of Compton scattered radiation?
questions.solution: Δλ = (h/mc)(1 - cosθ). The maximum occurs at θ = 180°, giving Δλmax = 2h/mc = 2 × 2.43 pm = 4.85 pm.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: X-rays with a wavelength of 0.150 nm are Compton scattered. At what scattering angle will the X-rays have a wavelength of 0.1506 nm?

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A photon of wavelength 3.56 pm undergoes Compton scattering from a free electron initially at rest. The wavelength of the scattered photon is 6.57 pm. Calculate the angle at which the recoil electron moves with respect to the direction of the incident photon.
questions.solution: First find the photon scattering angle: Δλ = 3.01 pm = 2.43(1 - cosθ), so cosθ = -0.239 and θ ≈ 104°. Momentum conservation gives p_ex = h/λi - (h/λf)cosθ and p_ey = -(h/λf)sinθ. Using h/pm units: p_ex = 0.281 + 0.152(0.239) = 0.317 and p_ey = -0.152(0.971) = -0.148. The recoil angle is tan⁻¹(-0.148/0.317) ≈ -25°, i.e. about 25° on the opposite side of the incident beam from the scattered photon.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Which part of a laser system is responsible for the directionality of the laser beam?
questions.solution: The cavity resonator (optical cavity) allows only waves travelling along its axis to build up through repeated reflection, producing a highly directional beam.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method to achieve population inversion?
questions.solution: Thermal equilibrium follows Boltzmann statistics and gives a lower population in the upper level, so it cannot produce inversion. Pumping, discharge and carrier injection are active methods.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: With reference to lasers, choose the wrong statement from the following.
options: The role of mirrors is to provide optical feedback for amplification.
Population inversion is a necessary condition for sustained stimulated emission.
Optical pumping is the only way to achieve population inversion.
In a semiconductor laser, a heavily doped p-n junction diode is used.
questions.solution: Population inversion can also be achieved by electrical discharge, carrier injection, chemical pumping or other methods, so optical pumping is not the only way.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: In a laser printer, the laser is primarily used to
questions.solution: The laser scans the charged photoconductor drum and discharges selected points, creating the electrostatic latent image that attracts toner. Fusing is done by heated rollers, not the laser.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Explain the following terms with reference to lasers: (a) spontaneous emission (b) stimulated emission. Give an example each.
questions.solution: (a) Spontaneous emission: an excited atom returns to a lower state on its own after its natural lifetime, emitting a photon of energy hf = E2 - E1 in a random direction and phase. Example: light emission from an LED. (b) Stimulated emission: an incident photon of suitable energy induces an excited atom to emit a second photon in phase, with the same frequency, polarization and direction. Example: the ruby laser. This is the process that produces coherent laser light.

images.alt: Spontaneous emission: an excited atom drops to a lower level and emits a photon in a random direction.
images.caption: Spontaneous emission: an excited atom drops to a lower level and emits a photon in a random direction.

images.alt: Stimulated emission: the incident photon triggers emission of an identical photon, giving two coherent photons.
images.caption: Stimulated emission: the incident photon triggers emission of an identical photon, giving two coherent photons.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A ruby laser delivers a 10 ns pulse of 1 MW average power. If the photons have a wavelength of 694.3 nm, how many photons are contained in the pulse? What is the spatial length of the pulse?

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: What are the essential components of a laser? Explain the role of each component in the production of laser light.
questions.solution: 1. Pumping system: supplies external energy (optical, electrical, chemical) to excite the active medium and create population inversion. 2. Active/lasing medium: provides the atoms, ions or molecules that undergo stimulated emission and determine the laser wavelength. 3. Resonant/optical cavity: two mirrors (one partially transmitting) provide optical feedback so emitted photons make repeated passes, amplifying stimulated emission and selecting the axial direction and wavelength.

images.alt: Essential laser components: pumping system, lasing medium and resonant cavity.
images.caption: Essential laser components: pumping system, lasing medium and resonant cavity.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Derive the relations between the Einstein coefficients A21, B21 and B12 for a two-level atomic system in thermal equilibrium.
questions.solution: At equilibrium, the rate of absorption equals the total rate of spontaneous and stimulated emission: N1B12ρ(ν) = N2A21 + N2B21ρ(ν). Hence ρ(ν) = A21/[B12(N1/N2) - B21]. Using the Boltzmann population ratio N2/N1 = (g2/g1)e^{-hν/kT}, ρ(ν) = (A21/B21)/[(g1B12/g2B21)e^{hν/kT} - 1]. Comparing with Planck's law ρ(ν) = (8πhν³/c³)/(e^{hν/kT} - 1) gives B12 = (g2/g1)B21 and A21/B21 = 8πhν³/c³.
questions.note: The official answer uses equal degeneracies (g1 = g2), which gives B12 = B21 and A21/B21 = 8πhν³/c³.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Choose the wrong statement from the following.
options: A single-mode step-index optical fibre consists of a core having a uniform refractive index.
A multimode step-index optical fibre consists of a core having a uniform refractive index.
The core diameter is larger for a single-mode step-index fibre than for a multimode step-index fibre.
Material dispersion in an optical fibre is due to the wavelength dependence of the core refractive index.
questions.solution: Single-mode fibres have a much smaller core (a few micrometres) than multimode fibres (typically 50-100 micrometres). The other three statements are correct.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Material dispersion in optical fibre communication can be reduced by
options: increasing the length of the fibre
questions.solution: Material dispersion arises because different wavelengths travel at different speeds. A source with a narrow spectral width contains fewer wavelengths, so pulse broadening is reduced.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Which dispersion mechanism is present in both single-mode and multimode fibres but depends strongly on the source spectral width?
questions.solution: Material dispersion depends on the wavelength dependence of the refractive index and therefore on the source linewidth. Intermodal dispersion requires multiple modes and is absent in single-mode fibre.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: A step-index optical fibre has core refractive index 1.48 and cladding refractive index 1.46. The core radius is 4 μm and the operating wavelength is 1550 nm. Calculate (a) the critical angle for total internal reflection at the core-cladding interface, (b) the numerical aperture, and (c) the maximum acceptance angle in air.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Define skip distance and derive an expression for it with a neat diagram.
questions.solution: Skip distance Ls is the axial distance between two successive reflections of a ray propagating through an optical fibre. Let d be the core diameter and θ1 the angle the ray makes with the fibre axis. Then Ls = d cotθ1. At the entrance, n0 sinθ0 = n1 sinθ1, so sinθ1 = (n0/n1) sinθ0. Therefore Ls = d sqrt(1 - sin²θ1)/sinθ1 = d sqrt(n1² - n0² sin²θ0)/(n0 sinθ0). For air (n0 = 1), Ls = d sqrt(n1² - sin²θ0)/sinθ0.

images.alt: Skip distance L_s for a ray travelling in a step-index fibre.
images.caption: Skip distance L_s for a ray travelling in a step-index fibre.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: With a necessary diagram, derive an expression for the angle of acceptance and numerical aperture.
questions.solution: A ray enters the core (index n1) from a medium n0 at angle θ0 to the axis, refracts at angle θ1, and strikes the core-cladding interface at the critical angle. Snell's law at entry gives n0 sinθ0 = n1 sinθ1. At the interface, sin(90° - θ1) = n2/n1, so cosθ1 = n2/n1 and sinθ1 = sqrt(n1² - n2²)/n1. Substituting gives n0 sinθ0 = sqrt(n1² - n2²). The acceptance angle is θ0 = sin⁻¹(sqrt(n1² - n2²)/n0), and NA = n0 sinθ0 = sqrt(n1² - n2²).

images.alt: Acceptance cone and numerical aperture of a step-index fibre.
images.caption: Acceptance cone and numerical aperture of a step-index fibre.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: With reference to optical fibre communication, what is material dispersion? Briefly explain.
questions.solution: Material dispersion is pulse broadening caused by the wavelength dependence of the refractive index of the core. An LED or other source emits a range of wavelengths; each wavelength travels at a slightly different group velocity, so the different components of a pulse arrive at different times and the pulse spreads. It is reduced by using a narrow-linewidth laser source.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: An optical fibre has a numerical aperture of 0.3. The refractive index of the cladding is 2% smaller than that of the core. Estimate the refractive indices of the core and the cladding.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: Obtain the relation between group velocity (vg) and phase velocity (vp) in a dispersive medium.
questions.solution: By definition vp = ω/k and vg = dω/dk. Since ω = k vp, vg = d(k vp)/dk = vp + k dvp/dk. Replacing k by 2π/λ and dk by -(2π/λ²)dλ gives vg = vp - λ dvp/dλ. Both forms show that group and phase velocities differ when vp depends on wavelength (a dispersive medium).

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.topic: Acceptance angle in a medium and modes
questions.question: A step-index optical fibre has a core diameter of 63.5 μm. When placed in air, the fibre's acceptance angle is 30°. (a) Calculate the acceptance angle of the fibre when it is immersed in a medium with refractive index 1.33. (b) Given an operating wavelength of 1300 nm, determine the approximate number of modes the fibre can support.
questions.solution: (a) NA = n0 sinθ0 = 1 × sin30° = 0.5. In the medium, sinθ0' = NA/n = 0.5/1.33 = 0.376, so θ0' ≈ 22.1°. (b) V = πd NA/λ = π × 63.5×10^-6 × 0.5/(1.30×10^-6) ≈ 76.7. The number of modes is approximately V²/2 ≈ 76.7²/2 ≈ 2.9×10^3 modes.

questions.subject: applied-physics
questions.question: With reference to optical fibre communication, what is intermodal dispersion?
questions.solution: In a multimode fibre, different modes follow different zigzag paths and therefore travel with different effective velocities along the axis. They reach the output at different times, broadening the pulse. This is intermodal dispersion. It is independent of the source spectral width and is absent in a single-mode fibre, where only one mode propagates.

images.alt: Intermodal dispersion: different ray paths travel different distances, so pulses spread.
images.caption: Intermodal dispersion: different ray paths travel different distances, so pulses spread.
